Name: Adam
Transcript: This is our last one. The season's over, more or less. Looking back over the year, what has it been like for you, keeping the plot?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: A year I didn't expect. I'll start with the bad bit, because it's the bit that matters. In September I did my back in. Lifting a sack of potatoes, of all things, the main crop. I'd lifted the lot, two rows, and I was carrying the last sack to the shed and something went at the bottom of my back, like a cable snapping. Down I went. Flat on the floor of the shed, among the potatoes. I couldn't get up. I lay there twenty minutes. Maureen found me in the end, she'd come to ask if I wanted some of her chard, and there's me on the floor like a beetle. She got Frank and Ken, and they got me up between them and into her car, and that was me. A fortnight on the settee.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What was that fortnight like?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: The worst since I retired. Worse than last winter. I lay there on the settee watching the ceiling, and it was the part left over again, only worse, because now I knew what I was missing. Last year I didn't know. This time I knew exactly. I knew the plot was down there with nobody on it. I could see it in my head going to ruin, the potatoes rotting in the sacks, the leaves blowing in the shed, and I thought, that's it. They'll be saying it at the gate. Told you. Another one who didn't last. Sixty-eight, and his back went, and that was him.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And then?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Then I went back. Two weeks to the day, walking with Pat's dad's old stick, it took me forty minutes from the flats. And I opened the shed. And the potatoes were in sacks. Not my sacks. Proper paper sacks, all lined up along the wall, tied at the top, and somebody had written on each one in marker pen, King Edward, King Edward, Desiree. And the plot had been forked over where I'd lifted them. Somebody had dug my plot. Frank and Ken, it turned out, and Maureen did the labels. Nobody'd said a word. I stood in my shed and I'll be honest with you, I had to sit down, and it wasn't my back.

Name: Adam
Transcript: It wasn't your back.

Name: Hollis
Transcript: No. I sat on Pat's chair in the shed and I had a minute. I'm not one for that, you know me by now. But I had a minute. Forty-one years I never let anybody do my job. You didn't. If another man had to finish your job it meant you couldn't do it, that's what it said. And a year ago, if somebody had dug my plot, that's what I'd have heard. I'd have been ashamed. I'd have taken it as them saying I wasn't up to it. And this time it was the other way round. Completely the other way round. You don't dig for somebody who's not one of you. You just don't.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Forty-one years you never let anybody do your job.

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Never. Not once, that I can think of. If I was off sick, which I hardly ever was, I'd come back and look at what they'd done on my buses and find something wrong with it. Every time. Because it had to be wrong, you see, or what was I for. That's how I thought. A man's what he can do. So you lie on a settee a fortnight and you can't do anything, and what are you then. That's what I was lying there thinking. And then I go down and they've done it, and it was right. It was all done right. The rows forked over proper. And I didn't look for anything wrong with it. I didn't want to.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What did you make of nobody saying anything?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Well, you don't, do you. That's how it's done. I tried to thank Frank, I went over to his shed, and I said, about the potatoes. And he didn't even look up. He said, your spuds were getting lonely. That's all. That's the nearest he'll ever get, Frank. And then in October they have a bonfire, all the old boys, they do it every year, everybody's prunings and the dead stuff. And I went down, still a bit stiff, and Ken handed me a rake. Just handed it me. Nobody said anything about it. But I knew what it meant.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What did it mean?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: That I'm one of the furniture now. That's how I'd put it. You're not new any more. You're not being watched. You're on the rake. There was me, Frank, Ken, and a couple of others, stood round the fire raking it in, not saying much, the smoke going in your eyes. Best night I've had in years. I'm not joking. Better than my leaving do, and they had a buffet at my leaving do.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Tell me about that night, at the bonfire.

Name: Hollis
Transcript: It was cold, clear, you could see the stars over the railway. The fire going right up, crackling, sparks going. We raked it in, kept it tidy. And nobody said much, like I say. But Frank told a story. About his wife, she's gone now, six years, how she used to come down to the bonfire with a tray of parkin every year, and he'd tell her off for bringing it, and she'd bring it anyway. And he went quiet after. And Ken put his hand on his shoulder, just for a second. And I was stood there with my rake, and I thought, I'm being let see this. That's what it was. I'm being let see this, because I'm one of them.

Name: Adam
Transcript: In March you said you'd like to walk through the gate one day and have them carry on talking. How is that now?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: They do. They carry on. There's not even a here he is now, half the time. But I'll tell you something I'm not proud of. A young lass has taken the plot by the gate. October. Purple hair, earrings all up her ear, a little dog. And the first Saturday she came down the path, we were stood at the gate, me and Frank and Ken, and we all stopped talking. All three of us. Me with them. And I heard us do it. I heard myself go quiet, the same as they did to me. And I thought, oh, here we go.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What was that like, hearing yourself go quiet?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: I didn't like it. And I did, a bit. Both. I didn't like it because I know what it's like from the other side, walking up that path with your neck burning. And I liked it a bit because, well, it meant I was on the right side of the gate now. That's the truth. So the next day I went over to her with a spare fork, I had two by then, and a bag of onion sets. And I told her her bed was too close to the hedge. Which is exactly what Frank did to me. I heard it come out of my mouth, and I thought, well, there it is. It goes round, doesn't it. It goes round.

Name: Adam
Transcript: How is she getting on, the young woman?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: She's all right. She's keen. Too keen, she does three hours and then can't move, like me in March. I told her that, and all. Pace yourself. She asked me last week what to do about her rhubarb, she's got an old rhubarb crown the last chap left. Just came over and asked. And I told her, and I didn't think less of her for asking. That's changed and all. In March I said you don't ask, you've not earned asking. And she asked, and I was glad she did. I'd have been glad if I'd asked Frank, I think, looking back. I'd have saved myself a lot of bother with them onions.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And home, with Pat, how has that been?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Better. I'll tell you a funny thing. The potatoes. Too many potatoes. Even with the back, I had more than we could eat in two years. So I put bags of them on the landing at the flats, with a note, help yourselves. And people I'd never spoken to in eleven years in that block knocked on my door to say thank you. The woman across the landing, I'd never known her name, she sent the bag back with a cake in it. A whole cake. And now we say hello. Eleven years, and it took a bag of potatoes.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Eleven years, and it took a bag of potatoes.

Name: Hollis
Transcript: It did. And Pat's noticed. She says I talk more. She says I come back from the plot with things to say. And I do. Who's got blight, whose shed blew over in the wind, what Frank said about the committee. I didn't have things to say before. I'd sit at my tea after I retired and there was nothing. What would I tell her? I watched the buses? At the depot I came home with stories every night, who'd done what, and she'd laugh. And then it stopped. A man needs a bit of news of his own, I think. Something that's happened to him.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Has Pat been down to the plot?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: She came in September, before the back, first time all year. She'd never come. She said it was my thing. I don't think she wanted to get in the way of it, the same as I'd been in her way. And she came and she sat on the bucket, Pat on my bucket, and I picked her a tomato off the plant, warm, and she ate it standing in the sun. And she said, that tastes of something. That's all she said. That tastes of something. I was proud. I'll admit that. I was proud.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You were proud.

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Aye. Because it was mine, that tomato, and she'd never seen anything of mine. Not really. At the depot she never came in, wives didn't. She'd hear about it, but she never saw it. Forty-one years she never saw what I did. And this time she came and sat in it. She sat in the middle of what I'd done and ate a bit of it. That's what it was. I'd never had that. I don't think I knew I wanted it till she was sat there.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And the winter ahead?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: I dread it a bit. I won't pretend. There's not much to do in December, a bit of digging, the shed roof. And I can feel the flat waiting for me. That's how it feels. Like the flat's sat up there on the ninth floor waiting for me to come back to it. I've started going down to the plot just to check the shed, which is daft. It doesn't need checking. It's a shed. But I go and check it.

Name: Adam
Transcript: The flat waiting for you. What's that like, as a feeling?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Like the bus station on a Sunday night. All the buses in, all lined up, lights off, nothing going anywhere. That's what I'm frightened of. Being a bus on a Sunday night. But I've got a plan. I'm doing the shed roof in December, felt and battens, I've got it all in. And Frank says the old boys come down in the winter anyway, they have a brew in his shed on a Wednesday, he's got a little gas ring. He said, you'll come Wednesdays. He didn't ask. He said. So maybe there's that. Maybe it won't be a Sunday night.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And your body, how is it now?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Stiff in the mornings. The back's mended, mostly, but it reminds me. I don't lift a full sack now, I do half sacks. Frank said, half sacks, you daft beggar, at your age. He's seventy-nine. He does half sacks and all, I've watched him. In March I'd have been ashamed of half sacks. Now I think, well, there's two trips instead of one. Two trips is more time down there. I've got the time.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What has the year changed for you, would you say?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: I talk more. That's the first thing. And I'm not the part left over. Not down there. Up in the flat, some days, still, I won't lie. But not down there. And the back. It'll go again. I'm sixty-eight, it'll go again, I know that now. In March that would've frightened the life out of me. But I know now that if it does, somebody'd lift my spuds. That's the difference. That's the whole difference, really. Somebody'd lift my spuds.
